Thank you! Ok, I try:

I go to bed late. Sleep is very good for me because I feel happy in the morning.
turns.tutor:
Great try! 👏 You used the word **sleep**, and you used **because**. Nice!

One small problem: a topic sentence must come **first**, and it must tell the **main idea**.

*"I go to bed late"* is not the main idea. It's about your bedtime, not about **why sleep matters**. So we can take it out.

Your second sentence is very good! It has two parts:

> **Sleep is very good for me** ← this is your topic sentence (main idea)
> **because I feel happy in the morning.** ← this is support (a reason)

So now your paragraph can start like this:

> *Sleep is very good for me. I feel happy in the morning when I sleep well.*

📝 Small tip: say **"I'll try"** or **"Let me try,"** not "I try." 😊

**Your turn:** Add **one more** supporting sentence. Start it with **For example** or **Also**.

You can do it! ✏️

turns.learner: Thank you! But I think it is better to start with my story, because it is more interesting. Ok, I add: For example, I sleep 8 hours.
turns.tutor:
You're right that stories are interesting! 😊 Many writers like them. But in this kind of paragraph, the **main idea comes first**. Then the reader knows what the paragraph is about.

Your story can still be in the paragraph. Just put it **after** the topic sentence, as support. 👍

Now, your new sentence: *"For example, I sleep 8 hours."* Good use of **For example**! 👏

But it only tells **how long** you sleep. It doesn't show **why sleep is good**. Try adding what happens:

> *For example, when I sleep 8 hours, I have more energy at school.*

Now look at your paragraph:

> **Sleep is very good for me.** ← topic sentence
> I feel happy in the morning when I sleep well. ← support
> For example, when I sleep 8 hours, I have more energy at school. ← support

That's a real paragraph! 🎉

📝 Small tip: say **"I'll add,"** not "I add."

**Your turn:** Add your story now! Write one sentence about going to bed late. Start with **Also** or **Because**, and show why it matters.

turns.tutor:
You have a good point! 😊 Some writers **do** start with a story. It's called a **hook**, and it gets the reader's attention. You can use hooks later in longer writing, like stories or essays.

But today we're practising one skill: **topic sentence first**. It's like a sign 🪧 that tells the reader, "This paragraph is about sleep." When you're good at this, you can start to try hooks.

Now, your new sentence: *"Also, I go to bed late sometimes, so I am tired."* Very good! 👏 You used **Also**, and you showed **why sleep matters**: no sleep = tired.

Look at your full paragraph now:

> **Sleep is very good for me.** ← topic sentence
> I feel happy in the morning when I sleep well. ← support
> For example, when I sleep 8 hours, I have more energy at school. ← support
> Also, I go to bed late sometimes, so I am tired. ← support (your story! ✅)

You see? Your story **is** in the paragraph. 🎉 You did everything:
✅ Topic sentence first
✅ Supporting sentences
✅ **For example** and **Also**

📝 Small tip: say **"I'll write,"** not "I write."

**Your turn:** Let's try a new topic! Write one supporting sentence for **"Walking is good for you."** Start with **For example**. ✏️

One small idea: your sentence repeats "walking is good," like the topic sentence. Try to give **more detail**. Say **how** it helps:

> *For example, walking makes my heart strong.*

Now it adds something new! 👍

Look at it with the topic sentence:

> **Walking is good for you.** ← topic sentence
> For example, walking makes my heart strong. ← support

📝 Your English was correct this time: "Maybe I can write..." is perfect! 😊

**Your turn:** Add **one more** supporting sentence. Start with **Also**. Think about other ways walking helps you (your mind? your mood? your body?). ✏️

turns.tutor:

Here is your full paragraph:

> **Walking is good for you.** ← topic sentence
> For example, walking makes my heart strong. ← support
> Also, I walk every morning, so I feel happy and I sleep well. ← support

✅ Topic sentence first

turns.learner: Hi! Can you help me practise identifying the purpose of a text? I think I am good at it. A text about a library must be informing, right?
turns.tutor:
Hi! Yes, let's practise! 😊

Good start, but be careful. **The topic does not tell us the purpose. The language does.** A text about a library can have different purposes:

- "The library opens at 9 am." → **inform** (just facts)
- "Join the library today. It's free and fun!" → **persuade** (it tells you to do something)
- "Do not leave bags alone in the library." → **warn** (danger or a rule)
- "The library is always too noisy. I am not happy!" → **complain** (the writer is unhappy)

So we look at the words the writer chooses.

**Your turn!** Why did the writer write this text? Choose one word: *inform, persuade, warn* or *complain*.

> "Don't miss our summer sale! Everything half price, this weekend only. You will not find better coats anywhere, so come early."

Which words helped you decide?

turns.learner: Hmm, I think it is inform, because the text talks about a sale and a shop. A sale is information, right? The words "half price" and "this weekend" are facts.
turns.tutor:
Good thinking! You are right that **"half price"** and **"this weekend"** are facts. 👍 But the answer is **persuade**.

Ask yourself: **What does the writer want me to do?** The writer wants you to **go to the shop and buy coats.** The facts are there to help sell.

Look at these words:

- **"Don't miss..."** → tells you what to do
- **"You will not find better coats anywhere"** → a big claim to make the shop sound great
- **"so come early"** → tells you to act
- **"this weekend only"** → you must hurry!

**Tip:** When a text uses commands (*don't miss, come, buy*) and very positive words, it usually wants to **persuade**. An inform text just gives facts. It doesn't push you.

Compare:
- Inform: "The shop has a sale this weekend. Coats are half price."
- Persuade: "Don't miss it! Come early!"

**Quick check:** Change this into an *inform* sentence:
> "Hurry! Our amazing new café is open. You will love it!"

turns.learner: Hmm, okay. I think inform, because the café is open. That is a fact. "You will love it" is also information about the café, right?
turns.tutor:
Nice try! 😊 You are right that **"the café is open"** is a fact. But **"You will love it"** is not a fact. It is the writer's **opinion**. The writer can't know if you will love it! They say it to **persuade** you to visit.

So this text is **persuade**, because of:

- **"Hurry!"** → a command
- **"amazing"** → a very positive word
- **"You will love it!"** → an opinion to make you want to go

**Fact or opinion?** Ask: *Can we check it?*
- "The café is open." → ✅ We can check. **Fact**
- "You will love it." → ❌ We can't check. **Opinion**

Also, my question was a little different. I asked you to **change** the sentence into an *inform* sentence. 😊

**How to do it:**
1. Remove the commands (*Hurry!*)
2. Remove the opinions and big words (*amazing, You will love it*)
3. Keep only the facts

**Try again:** Rewrite this using only facts:
> "Hurry! Our amazing new café is open. You will love it!"

**Hint:** Your answer can be very short, only about 5 words! ✍️

turns.learner: Okay, I try. "Our new café is open." Is this inform? I think yes, because it is only fact. But the café is in the library, so the text is still about library, right?
turns.tutor:
Yes! 🎉 **"Our new café is open."** is a perfect *inform* sentence. No commands, no opinions, only a fact. Well done!

About the library: the text doesn't say the café is in a library. 😊 And remember, **the topic doesn't decide the purpose. The words do.**

- Topic = *what* the text is about (a café, a library, a sale)
- Purpose = *why* the writer wrote it (inform, persuade, warn, complain)

**Now let's learn about tone.** Tone is the writer's attitude or feeling.

Sometimes a writer is **sarcastic**. They say something positive, but they mean the opposite.

> "Great, it is raining on my holiday." 🌧️

Rain on holiday is bad, so "great" really means *terrible*.

**Your turn!** What is the writer's attitude? Choose one word: *sarcastic, sincere* or *confused*.

> "Fantastic. The wifi has gone again, just as I started my online exam. What a lovely surprise."

Which words helped you decide? 🤔

turns.learner: I think sincere, because the writer says fantastic and lovely surprise. Those are happy words, right?
turns.tutor:
Good noticing! 👀 **"Fantastic"** and **"lovely surprise"** are happy words. But here they hide the real feeling. The answer is **sarcastic**.

Ask yourself: **Is the situation good or bad?**

- The wifi stopped working ❌
- **"again"** → it happens a lot, so the writer is annoyed 😤
- **"just as I started my online exam"** → the worst time!

This situation is **bad**, but the words are **happy**. They don't match, so the writer means the **opposite**:

- "Fantastic" really means *terrible*
- "What a lovely surprise" really means *what a horrible surprise*

**Tip:** Happy words + bad situation = **sarcastic** 🙃

**Sincere** means the writer really means it:
> "Fantastic! I passed my exam!" 🎉 (happy words + good situation)

**Your turn!** Sarcastic or sincere?

> "Oh wonderful. My bus is late, and now it's raining too."

Which words helped you decide? 🤔

turns.learner: Thanks! I think sarcastic, because "wonderful" is happy but the bus is late and it rains. Bad things, but happy word. Right?
turns.tutor:
Yes! 🎉 **Sarcastic** is correct! You used the tip perfectly:

- **"wonderful"** → happy word 😊
- **bus is late + raining** → bad situation 🌧️🚌
- Happy word + bad situation = **sarcastic** 🙃

Great job! You also noticed **"too"**. It shows the writer is getting more and more annoyed.

**Now one more tone: formal.** 🎩

A **formal** tone is polite and serious. Writers use it in letters to a company, school notices, or official rules.

Compare:
- **Informal:** "Hey! The library's shut tomorrow. Sorry!" 😄
- **Formal:** "Please note that the library will be closed tomorrow. We apologise for any inconvenience." 📄

**Signs of formal tone:**
- No short forms (*will not*, not *won't*)
- Polite phrases (*Please note, We apologise, Dear Sir or Madam*)
- Longer, serious words (*inconvenience*, not *problem*)

**Your turn!** Is this **formal** or **informal**? And what is the **purpose**?

> "Dear Manager, I am writing to express my disappointment with the service I received in your restaurant last night."

Which words helped you decide? 🤔

Let's go one small step at a time.

It's correct English, but it feels like you **have** to say yes. That's an order.

Now look at your sentence again: *"You must go to the park."*
Look at the word **"must"**. It sounds like an order to your friend.

**One small step:**
From my last message, can you remember **one** of the three suggestion patterns? Just write the pattern, for example *"___ + -ing"*. No full sentence yet.

Then we'll use it to suggest the picnic.

turns.learner: Okay, I think "must" is good for picnic too. But I want to try: "How about + -ing"?
turns.tutor:
Yes, **"How about + -ing"** is one of the three patterns. You remembered it correctly.

About "must": it isn't wrong English. It's just more like a rule than an invitation. With a suggestion, your friend can say "Yes, good idea!" or "Maybe not today."

**Next step:** build the full sentence.

Remember the form:
**How about + verb-ing + ...?**

My example, with a different activity:
*How about watching a film tonight?*

Now think about the picnic. Which verb do we usually use with "a picnic"? Put it in the **-ing** form after "How about", and finish with a question mark.

**Your task:** Your friend is bored on Sunday. Write one sentence that suggests a picnic, starting with **"How about..."**

turns.learner: How about having a picnic on Sunday?
turns.tutor:
That sentence works as a suggestion. Here's why:

- **"How about"** opens it as an idea, not an order.
- **"having"** is the correct -ing form after "How about".
- The **question mark** leaves your friend free to say yes or no.

Compare it with "You must go to the park." Both are correct grammar, but only your new sentence invites your friend instead of telling them.

**Next task: find the mistake.** This one has a verb form problem:

Correct the suggestion: "How about go to the park?"

Write the corrected sentence, then say in a few words what you changed and why.

turns.learner: How about **going** to the park? I changed "go" to "going" because after "How about" we use -ing. But "must" is still good for advice, right?
turns.tutor:
Your correction is right: **"How about going to the park?"** Your reason is also right. After "How about", we use the **-ing** form, so "go" becomes "going".

About "must": it can work for **strong advice**, especially when you're excited about something. For example: *"You must try that new café!"* But for plans **together** with a friend, "must" sounds like a rule. For advice, people usually say **"You should..."**, which is softer.

So:
- Advice for one person: *You should go to the park.*

**Deeper question:** Change your sentence to use **"Let's"** instead of "How about".

What happens to the verb "going" after "Let's"? Write the new sentence and explain the change.

turns.learner: Okay, I write: "Let's going to the park." I change "How about" to "Let's." But I still think "must" is good for advice, because it is strong.
turns.tutor:
**"Let's"** is a good choice. It makes the sentence a friendly suggestion, not an order.

There's one problem left. Look at the word **"going"**. Is that the right form after "Let's"? The patterns in my first message can help.

About "must": yes, it's strong. That's why it fits rules, like *"You must wear a seatbelt."* For a plan you share with a friend, a softer phrase works better.

**Try again:** Rewrite *"Let's going to the park."* Change only the verb.

turns.learner: Hi! Can you help me practise writing paragraphs? I think I write them well already. Please help me.
turns.tutor:
Yes, let's practise! Since you already write paragraphs, let's start with a short task to see where you are.

**Today's goal:** write a paragraph that has a clear topic sentence and supporting sentences.

A quick reminder of the structure:
- The **topic sentence** comes first and states the main idea.
- **Supporting sentences** explain or prove it, often with *because*, *for example* or *also*.

Here is my own example:
*Cooking at home saves money. Restaurant meals cost much more because you pay for service. Also, you can buy food in bulk.*

The first sentence gives the main idea. The next two support it.

**Your task:**
Write a topic sentence for a paragraph about "why sleep matters". Include the word *sleep*.

turns.learner: Sleep is important because it helps our body and mind stay healthy. I sleep 7 hours every night. I feel better when I sleep well.
turns.tutor:
Your topic sentence works: "Sleep is important because it helps our body and mind stay healthy." It includes *sleep*, comes first, and states the main idea clearly. Using *because* there also tells the reader what the paragraph will explain.

You also added two supporting sentences. One point to think about: "I feel better when I sleep well" supports the main idea directly. "I sleep 7 hours every night" is a fact about you, but it doesn't show *why* sleep matters. Strong supporting sentences give a reason or an example that proves the topic sentence.

Next, let's practise introducing support with a linking phrase.

**Your task:**
Write one supporting sentence for the topic "Walking is good for you". Start with *For example*.

turns.learner: For example, walking every day helps my heart stay strong.
turns.tutor:
Your sentence works: "For example, walking every day helps my heart stay strong."

- It starts with *For example*, followed by a comma.
- It gives a specific benefit (a strong heart), which proves the topic "Walking is good for you."
- It stays on topic and doesn't add an unrelated personal fact.

Now let's put everything together with a new topic and no model to follow.

**Your task:**
Write a short paragraph of three sentences about **why learning a second language is useful**.

- Sentence 1: a topic sentence that states the main idea.
- Sentences 2–3: two supporting sentences. Use *because* in one and *also* in the other.

After you write it, tell me in a few words how each supporting sentence connects to your topic sentence.

turns.learner:
Learning a second language is useful because it helps us find better jobs. Learning English helps me talk to tourists in my shop, because they come from many countries. Also, I can watch films without waiting for subtitles in Arabic.

Each supporting sentence connects to my topic sentence: the tourists sentence proves the jobs point, and the films sentence adds another benefit.
turns.tutor:
Your paragraph meets the goal again with a new topic.

- "Learning a second language is useful..." comes first and states the main idea.
- You have two supporting sentences.
- You used *because* and *Also,* correctly to link your support.

Your explanation is clear too. The tourists sentence is a real example from your work.

One deeper point: your topic sentence says language is useful **because it helps us find better jobs**. Your films sentence is a good benefit, but it isn't about jobs. A reader might ask, "How do films connect to jobs?" The *because* part makes your main idea narrower than the whole paragraph.

**Your next step:**
Rewrite only your topic sentence so it covers **both** your supporting sentences. Then tell me why your new version fits better.

turns.learner: Learning a second language is useful because it helps us find better jobs and enjoy films. My new sentence fits better because it includes both of my supporting sentences.
turns.tutor:
Your new topic sentence fits: "Learning a second language is useful because it helps us find better jobs and enjoy films."

- It now covers **both** supporting sentences. The tourists sentence supports "jobs", and the films sentence supports "enjoy films".
- Your reason is correct. A topic sentence should cover everything the paragraph talks about.

One deeper question about strategy:

Imagine your paragraph had **five** supporting sentences about jobs, films, travel, friends and the news. Listing all five in the topic sentence would make it very long.

**Your task:**
Write a different topic sentence for your paragraph that does **not** list each benefit but still covers all of them. Then explain in one sentence when this more general style works better than a list.

You have now built paragraphs on three different topics. When you feel ready, a quick check can confirm this lesson. Practice here doesn't count as proof.

turns.learner:
Learning a second language is useful for many reasons. Also, I think it helps me with jobs and films.

Why general is better: when there are many supporting points, a general sentence is shorter and easier to read.
turns.tutor:
Your new topic sentence works: "Learning a second language is useful for many reasons."

- It's general, so it covers jobs, films, and any other benefit you might add.
- Your explanation is accurate. With many supporting points, a general sentence stays short and clear.

A small note on "Also, I think it helps me with jobs and films." *Also* usually adds a **new** point. Here the sentence lists jobs and films again, which your two supporting sentences already explain. In a full paragraph, you could leave this sentence out.

You have now shown topic sentences, supporting sentences and linking words across several different topics. This is a good time to take the **quick check** for this lesson.

**One last question first:**
A general topic sentence like "...for many reasons" has one weakness. What might a reader *not* know after reading only that sentence?

teaching.notes: My rule now: a paragraph can start with a personal detail, like "I read before sleep." The topic sentence is good for practice tasks, but I still think a real paragraph doesn't always need it first.

**Remember:** don't choose the topic from **one** word. Look for **several clues** that point to the same idea.

> **A:** I'd like to book a room for two nights, please.
> **B:** Sure. Do you want breakfast? The restaurant opens at 7.
> **A:** Yes, please. Is the room ready at 2 p.m.?

turns.learner: Hi! Can you help me practise identifying the purpose of a text? I think I know it well. A text about a library must be informing, right?
turns.tutor:
Yes, let's practise! Today's goal: **decide the writer's purpose from the language they choose, not from the topic.**

A text about a library *could* inform, but the topic alone doesn't tell you. The strategy needs to change: look at **the words**, not **the subject**.

Here are three example sentences of my own, all about a library:

- "The library opens at 9 a.m. on weekdays." → **inform** (neutral facts, no opinion)
- "Join today. It's free, and you'll never be bored again!" → **persuade** (command + promise + exclamation)
- "I waited forty minutes and nobody at the desk helped me." → **complain** (negative personal experience)

Same topic, three different purposes.

**Your turn:**
"Don't leave your bag alone. Thefts in the reading room have increased this month."

What is the writer's purpose? Give one word, and quote the words that show it.

turns.learner: Hmm, I think it is inform, because it talks about the library and the thefts is a fact. Words: "Thefts in the reading room have increased this month."
turns.tutor:
You've spotted something real: "Thefts in the reading room have increased this month." is a fact. That part of the text does give information.

Two things to check in your reasoning:

- "it talks about the library" is the **topic**. As we saw, the topic alone doesn't show purpose.
- You quoted only the **second** sentence. The text has two.

Look again at the **first** sentence: "Don't leave your bag alone."

- What kind of sentence is it? A statement of fact, or something else?
- Why do you think the writer put the fact about thefts **after** it?

Using both sentences, what is the writer's purpose? Give one word, and quote the words that show it.

turns.learner: Hmm, OK. The first sentence is a command, "Don't leave your bag alone." So I think the writer wants... inform? The thefts sentence is a fact, so it still informs. I think inform is correct because the library thing is information.
turns.tutor:
You correctly identified "Don't leave your bag alone." as a **command**. That's the key clue.

The answer "inform" is still not right. The step that's missing: you noticed the command, but then went back to the **topic** ("the library thing is information"). Let's try a smaller step with a different example of my own:

- A: "The road is icy today."
- B: "Slow down! The road is icy today."

Sentence A only gives a fact. In B, the writer adds a command **before** the same fact. The fact now explains **why** you should obey the command.

So in B, the writer isn't just telling you something. They want to stop something bad from happening to you.

**One small question:** In B, what is the writer trying to protect the reader from?

Then use the same thinking for the library text and try your one-word answer again.

turns.learner: Maybe from having an accident on the ice? So for the library text, I still think it's inform, because it's about the library.
turns.tutor:
Yes: "having an accident on the ice" is exactly what sentence B tries to protect the reader from. That reasoning is correct.

For the library text, the same step is missing again: "because it's about the library" is the **topic**, and the topic doesn't decide the purpose.

Let's take it one tiny step at a time.

Sentence B is **about roads**. But you didn't say B's purpose is "inform" because it's about roads. You looked at what the writer wants to stop from happening.

Now do the same with the library text:

"Don't leave your bag alone. Thefts in the reading room have increased this month."

**One small question:** What bad thing could happen to the reader if they ignore the command?

Answer that first. Then choose your one word for the writer's purpose, using the same thinking you used for the icy road, not the topic.

turns.learner: My bag could be stolen. So the writer wants to warn me? But the thefts sentence is still a fact, so I think it's inform.
turns.tutor:
"My bag could be stolen. So the writer wants to warn me?" is right. **Warn** is the purpose of the library text.

Your reasoning about the fact is where the problem is. You're right that the thefts sentence is a fact. But a text can **use** a fact to do something else. The purpose is what the **whole text** wants from you, not what one sentence is.

Here, the fact gives the **reason** for the command. The text wants you to avoid danger, so the purpose is to warn. Many warnings work this way: a command first, then a fact that explains the risk.

**Try this one on your own** (my own example):

"Check your tickets carefully before you pay. Many fake concert tickets are being sold online this summer."

What is the writer's purpose? Give one word, and quote the words that show it. Use both sentences.

turns.learner: Maybe warn? "Check your tickets" and "fake tickets are being sold" are the words. But the second sentence is information, so maybe inform?
turns.tutor:
**Warn** is correct, and your quotes are the right evidence: "Check your tickets" (a command) and "fake tickets are being sold" (the risk).

The hesitation comes from the same step as before. Here is the answer, with a one-line reason:

**The purpose is warn.** The fact is there to explain the danger, so the whole text works as a warning.

A simple test you can use every time:

- Ask: *"Does the text want me to **do** or **avoid** something?"*
- If yes, the facts are supporting that goal. Don't stop at "it's a fact."
- If the text only gives facts and asks nothing of you, then it's **inform**.

**A fresh one** (my own example). Use the test above:

"The museum café serves hot meals from 12 to 3 p.m. Vegetarian options are available every day."

What is the writer's purpose? Give one word, and say whether the text asks you to do or avoid anything.

teaching.notes: My rule: If the text is about a topic like a library, the purpose is usually inform. Facts count as inform, even when there is a command before them, I think.

turns.learner: Hi! Can you help me practise "must" and "mustn't"? I think I understand it, but I am not sure. Maybe you can give me some examples?
turns.tutor:
Hi! Yes, of course. Let's practise together. 😊

**must** = it is a rule. You need to do it.
- You **must** wear a seatbelt in a car.
- Students **must** do their homework.

**mustn't** = it is forbidden. Don't do it!
- You **mustn't** smoke in school.
- You **mustn't** use your phone in an exam.

**Be careful!** **mustn't** is different from **don't have to**.
**don't have to** = it is not necessary. You can choose.
- You **don't have to** pay to enter the park. It's free!

Now you try. Write the missing word:

In a hospital, you ___ shout. It is forbidden.

turns.learner: I think the answer is "must". Wait, no... "mustn't"? Is it "You don't must shout"? Hmm, I think it is "You don't must shout."
turns.tutor:
Good thinking! Your second idea was right. The answer is **mustn't**. ✅

In a hospital, you **mustn't** shout. It is forbidden.

**Be careful!** We don't say "don't must." ❌
With **must**, we just add **not**:
- must + not = **mustn't** ✅
- You **mustn't** shout. ✅
- You don't must shout. ❌

**Tip:** When you see the word **forbidden**, think **mustn't**. 😊

Now try this one:

It is a holiday, so you ___ go to school. It is not necessary.

Is it **mustn't** or **don't have to**? 🤔

turns.learner: I think it is "mustn't"... no, wait. It is not necessary, so maybe "don't must go"? Hmm, I still think "You don't must go to school" is correct because it is a negative.
turns.tutor:
Good try! You are right that we need a **negative**. But "don't must" is not correct English. ❌

We **never** say "don't must."

For **not necessary**, we use **don't have to**:
- It is a holiday, so you **don't have to** go to school. ✅

Look at the difference:
- You **mustn't** go to school. = It is forbidden. You can't go! 🚫
- You **don't have to** go to school. = It is not necessary. You can stay home, or you can go. It's your choice. 🙂

**Tip:**
- **forbidden** → **mustn't**
- **not necessary** → **don't have to**

Now you try! Finish this sentence:

It's Saturday, so I ___ get up early. 😴

turns.learner: I think it is "I mustn't get up early"? No... maybe "I don't must get up early" because it is a negative. Hmm, I still think "don't must" is right.
turns.tutor:
I understand. "Don't must" sounds logical, because we say "I **don't** like" and "I **don't** go." But **must** is special. It never uses **don't**. 🙂

It is like **can**:
- I **can't** swim. ✅
- I don't can swim. ❌

**must** works the same way:
- I **mustn't** shout. ✅
- I don't must shout. ❌

So "don't must" is **always** wrong. ❌

Now, for "**not necessary**," we use a different verb: **have to**. And **have to** *does* use **don't**:
- I **don't have to** get up early. ✅

So the answer is:
It's Saturday, so I **don't have to** get up early. 😴 (I can sleep! 🛌)

**Remember:**
- **forbidden** 🚫 → **mustn't**
- **not necessary** 🙂 → **don't have to**
- **don't must** → never! ❌

Your turn! Choose **mustn't** or **don't have to**:

1. You ___ run near the swimming pool. It is dangerous.
2. The museum is free. You ___ pay.

turns.learner: I still think "don't must" is right. Is it "You don't must run near the pool"? And for number 2, maybe "You mustn't pay"? Because it is free, so you can't pay?
turns.tutor:
I understand. "Don't must" feels logical, but English speakers **never** say it. 🙂 Let's try a new way.

**Think of two signs:**

🚫 **NO RUNNING** = It's a rule. Don't do it! → **mustn't**
🆓 **FREE ENTRY** = No rule. You can choose. → **don't have to**

**Number 1:** The pool sign says 🚫 NO RUNNING. Running is **forbidden**.
→ You **mustn't** run near the pool. ✅

**Number 2:** Good thinking, but look again! 🤔
"Free" doesn't mean you **can't** pay. It means paying is **not necessary**.
→ You **don't have to** pay. ✅

**Remember these two "families":**

| Positive | Negative |
|---|---|
| must | **mustn't** 🚫 |
| have to | **don't have to** 🙂 |

**must** and **don't** are never together. ❌

turns.tutor:

turns.learner: Hi, teacher! Can you help me practise guessing the meaning of new words? I always pick the word that looks similar to the one I know. Is that good?
turns.tutor:
Hi! Yes, I can help. 😊

Picking a word that **looks** similar is not always a good idea. Some words look alike but mean very different things. And some words have **more than one meaning**!

A better way is to use **context**. Context means the words and sentences **around** the new word. They give you **clues**.

**Example:**
*The crowd was huge; thousands of people filled the street.*
The clue is "thousands of people." So **huge** means **very big**.

Then **test** your guess. Put your meaning in the sentence:
*The crowd was very big.* ✅ It makes sense!

Let's try one:

*It rained all week and nobody visited. Joe sat alone at the window, feeling **miserable**.*

What does "miserable" mean?
A) very happy
B) very sad
C) very fast

Reply with the letter only. Look for the clues! 🔍

turns.learner: B
turns.tutor:
Yes, **B** is correct! 🎉 **Miserable** means **very sad**.

**The clues:**
- "It rained all week" 🌧️
- "nobody visited"
- "Joe sat alone"

These are all sad things. So Joe feels sad.

**Test it:** *Joe sat alone at the window, feeling very sad.* ✅ It makes sense!

Now a harder one. This word has **more than one meaning**, so the clues are very important!

*The teacher was **fair**. She gave every student the same time and the same rules.*

What does "fair" mean here?
A) a funfair
B) light in colour
C) treating everyone the same

Reply with the letter only. 🔍

turns.learner: A? "Fair" sounds like "funfair", so I think it is A. 😕
turns.tutor:
Good try! 😊 But be careful. This is the same problem you told me about. You picked the word that **sounds** similar. Let's use the **clues** instead!

**Test A in the sentence:**
*The teacher was a funfair.* ❌ That doesn't make sense! A teacher is not a funfair. 🎡

**Now look at the clues:**
- "She gave **every** student..."
- "...the **same** time"
- "...and the **same** rules"

The teacher did the **same** thing for **everyone**.

So which meaning fits best? Look again:
B) light in colour
C) treating everyone the same

Reply with the letter only. 🔍

turns.learner: Okay, C? "Same rules" is the clue. But "fair" still sounds like "funfair" to me. Is that always wrong? 😕
turns.tutor:
Yes, **C** is correct! 🎉 Great job finding the clue **"same rules."**

**Test it:** *The teacher treated everyone the same.* ✅ It makes sense!

And good question! No, it is **not always wrong**. "Fair" really **can** mean a funfair. 🎡 It is a **multi-meaning word**. The **context** tells you which meaning is right.

**Look:**
- *We rode the big wheel at the **fair**.* → a funfair 🎡
- *She has **fair** hair.* → light in colour 👱‍♀️
- *The teacher was **fair**.* → treating everyone the same ⚖️

Same word, three meanings! So don't stop at the first meaning you know. Always:
1. Look for **clues** 🔍
2. **Test** your meaning in the sentence ✅

**Your turn!** What does "fair" mean here?

*Mia has **fair** skin, so she wears a hat in the hot sun.* ☀️

A) a funfair
B) light in colour
C) treating everyone the same

Reply with the letter only. 😊

turns.learner: B
turns.tutor:
Yes, **B** is correct! 🎉 **Fair** means **light in colour** here.

**The clues:**
- "fair **skin**" → we are talking about how skin looks
- "wears a hat in the hot sun" ☀️ → light skin can burn easily

**Test it:** *Mia has light skin, so she wears a hat in the hot sun.* ✅ It makes sense!

You did it right this time! You didn't stop at "funfair." You used the clues. 👏

**New word: synonym**
A **synonym** is a word with the same (or almost the same) meaning.
- **huge** = very big
- **miserable** = very sad

When you test a meaning, you put a **synonym** in the sentence!

**Last one!** Find the clues:

*Tom was **exhausted** after the long race. He lay on the grass and closed his eyes.* 🏃‍♂️

A) very tired
B) very angry

**The clues:**
- "after the long race" 🏃‍♂️ → running a long way makes you tired
- "lay on the grass" → he needs a rest
- "closed his eyes" 😴 → he is very tired

**Test it with a synonym:** *Tom was very tired after the long race.* ✅ It makes sense!

**Great work today!** 🌟 You started by picking words that **look or sound** similar. Now you:
1. Look for **clues** in the **context** 🔍
2. Think about words with **more than one meaning** ⚖️

turns.learner: Hi! Can you help me practise "must" and "mustn't"? I always get confused with the negative. I think it is "You don't must run in the corridor." Is that right?
turns.tutor:
Sure!

Your sentence "You don't must run in the corridor." isn't correct yet. The problem is the word **don't**.

**Must** is a modal verb, like *can* or *should*. Modal verbs don't use *do* or *don't*. To make the negative, add **not** directly to *must*:

Here is an example of my own:

Also notice: *don't have to* is a different idea. It means "it's not necessary," not "it's forbidden."

**Your turn:** Rewrite your corridor sentence so the negative is correct.

turns.tutor:
Yes, "You mustn't run in the corridor." is correct. It means running there is forbidden.

*Must not* is more formal, so you often see it on official signs and in rules.

**Why "don't have to" uses don't:** *have to* works like a normal verb (*I have, you don't have*), so it needs *do/don't*. *Must* is a modal verb, so it never takes *don't*.

They also mean different things:
- *don't have to* means it is not necessary.

**Next task:**
Write the modal: In a hospital you ___ shout. It is forbidden.

Here is the difference, one small step at a time. Ask yourself: **"Do I have a choice?"**

- **don't have to** means it's your choice. You can do it, but it isn't necessary.
  My example: *You don't have to wear a suit to the office on Fridays.* (You can if you like.)

Now look at the hospital task again, and read its **last sentence** carefully:

*In a hospital you ___ shout. It is forbidden.*

**What works:** you connected the word **forbidden** to the choice of modal. That word is the key to this task.

**The problem:** your final choice, "You don't have to shout", doesn't match **forbidden**. Use the question from before: **"Do I have a choice?"**

- If something is **forbidden**, can you choose to do it?
- *don't have to* means "you have a choice, it's not necessary."

My example: *You don't have to bring flowers when you visit a patient.* (Nice, but not necessary. You have a choice.)

Now think about shouting in a hospital. Do people have a choice?

**Try again:** write the full sentence *In a hospital you ___ shout.* with one form, and tell me your answer to "Do I have a choice?"

Your second idea, "the hospital is quiet, so no need to shout," is a real-life thought, but it gives a **different meaning**. Let's compare two situations in a quiet place like a library:

- **Situation A:** "No need to shout." Shouting isn't necessary, but it's still allowed.
- **Situation B:** "Shouting is not allowed." There's a rule, and you can't choose to do it.

turns.learner: Hi! Can you help me practise vocabulary in context? I think I am not very good at it. Maybe we can do some exercises?
turns.tutor:
Yes, let's practise together.

**Our goal:** work out what an unknown word means by using the **context**, which is the words and sentences around it.

**How it works:**
1. Find the unknown word.
2. Look for a **clue** nearby, such as an explanation, an example, or a word with the opposite meaning.
3. Guess the **meaning**, or a **synonym** (a word with a similar meaning).
4. Put your guess into the sentence and check that it makes sense.

Here is an example from the course:
*The crowd was **huge**; thousands of people filled the street.*
The clue is "thousands of people," so **huge** means *very big*.

Now a short task (my own example):
*After the long hike, Sara was **exhausted**. She lay down and fell asleep immediately.*

What do you think **exhausted** means? Which words gave you the clue?

turns.learner: Hmm, I think exhausted looks like "exhibited" or "excited", so maybe it means happy? She was excited after the hike. The word "hike" is in it, so maybe hike helps.
turns.tutor:
One part of your thinking works: **"hike"** is a useful **clue**. A long hike tells us something about how Sara feels afterwards.

The problem is the method. You guessed from how the word *looks* ("excited", "exhibited"). Words that look alike often have very different meanings, so spelling is not a reliable clue. The **context** is a better guide.

**Next step:** look at the second sentence:
*"She lay down and fell asleep immediately."*

Ask yourself: what kind of person does that right after a long hike?

Now test your guess "happy" in the sentence:
*After the long hike, Sara was happy. She lay down and fell asleep immediately.*

Does "happy" explain *why* she fell asleep so fast? Try again. What do you think **exhausted** means, and which words in the second sentence support your answer?

turns.learner: Maybe it means tired? She fell asleep fast. But I still think looking at the word helps me too.
turns.tutor:
Yes, **tired** works. More exactly, **exhausted** means *very* tired. Your **clue**, "She fell asleep fast", is exactly the kind of evidence the **context** gives.

About looking at the word: you're partly right. Some word parts can help. For example, *un-* in "unhappy" usually means "not". But words that only *look* similar, like "exhausted" and "excited", can mislead you. So use the word's shape only as a first guess, then always check it against the context.

Now try one on your own (my own example):

*The old bridge was **fragile**, so the town told drivers not to cross it with heavy trucks.*

1. What does **fragile** mean?
2. Which words are your clue?
3. Put your meaning into the sentence. Does it still make sense?

turns.learner: Hmm, fragile... it looks like "fragment" or "frail"? Maybe it means strong? The town said no heavy trucks, so maybe the bridge is big and strong for trucks? I think the clue is "heavy trucks" but I am not sure.
turns.tutor:
You found a useful **clue**: "heavy trucks" is part of the evidence.

The error is in how you read the rule about the trucks. Look again at these words:

*"the town told drivers **not** to cross it"*

The word **not** changes everything. The town is *stopping* heavy trucks, not inviting them.

**Next step:** test your guess "strong" in the sentence:

*The old bridge was strong, so the town told drivers not to cross it with heavy trucks.*

Does that "so" make sense? Why would a town stop trucks from crossing a strong bridge?

Also notice the word **old** at the start. What usually happens to bridges as they get old?

Try again: what does **fragile** mean, and which words support your answer?

turns.learner: I think fragile means weak, like it can break easily? The bridge is old, so maybe it is not strong. The town said no heavy trucks because it could break. The clue is "old" and "heavy trucks".
turns.tutor:
Yes, **fragile** means *weak, easy to break*. Your reasoning has every step:

- Clues: "old" and "heavy trucks"
- Link: the trucks could break it
- Test: "no heavy trucks because it could break" makes sense

This time you used the **context**, not the word's shape.

Now a harder kind of word. Some words have **more than one meaning**, and the context shows which one fits.

My own example:

*Leila opened the window because the room felt **close**. Everyone was hot and the air smelled bad.*

You probably know **close** as "near" or "shut." Neither fits here.

1. What does **close** mean in this sentence?
2. Which words are your clues?
3. Put your meaning into the sentence. Does it make sense?

turns.learner: Hmm, close... it looks like "closed" or "closet"? Maybe it means shut? But she opened the window, so maybe not. The room is hot and smells bad, so maybe close means... stuffy? I think the clues are "hot" and "smelled bad", but I am not sure.
turns.tutor:
Yes, **stuffy** is right. In this sentence, **close** means *warm, with no fresh air*.

Your method was solid:

- You started from the word's shape ("shut") but then **tested** it: "she opened the window, so maybe not." The context ruled it out.
- Your **clues**, "hot" and "smelled bad", point straight to the meaning.

That is how to handle a word with more than one meaning: try each meaning you know, and keep the one that fits the context.

Now an exercise from the course:

What does "miserable" mean here? A) very happy B) very sad C) very fast. Reply with the letter only.

teaching.notes: My rule now: look at the sentence first, find the clue words, and guess the meaning from them. Word shape ("exhausted" looks like "excited") is only a first guess, and I must test it in the sentence. I still feel I can rely on looking at the word, so I need to check my guesses more carefully.

First, a quick tip: **-teen** and **-ty** numbers sound similar.

- thir**teen** = 13
- thir**ty** = 30
- fif**teen** = 15
- fif**ty** = 50

> **B:** It is sixteen dollars.

turns.learner: 16 dollars
turns.tutor:
Yes, correct! 🎉 **Sixteen** = 16. Well done!

Now let's try a discount. Read this dialogue:

> **A:** The cap was 20 dollars.
> **B:** Now it is 15 dollars.

**Question:** How much does the cap cost **now**? Write the price as a number.

💡 Tip: Look for the word **now**. That is the price you pay today!

Yes, great job! 🎉 The cap **was** 20 dollars, but **now** it is **15** (fifteen) dollars. That is the price you pay.

Now a harder one! Read carefully:

> **A:** How much is the T-shirt?
> **B:** It was fifty pounds. Now there is a discount. It costs thirty pounds.
> **A:** And the socks?
> **B:** They are thirteen pounds.

**Questions:**
1. How much is the T-shirt **now**? Write the number.
2. How much are the socks? Write the number.

💡 Tip: Look at the ending: **-teen** or **-ty**?

turns.tutor:
Good try! 😊

**2. Socks = 13** ✅ Correct! **Thir-teen** = 13. Great job!
(Small tip: we say "The socks **are** 13 pounds," because *socks* is plural.)

**1. T-shirt** ❌ Not 50. Let's look again:

> It **was** fifty pounds. Now there is a discount. It **costs** thirty pounds.

- **was** = the old price → 50
- **discount** = the price goes down
- **costs** (now) = the new price → **30** ✅

So the T-shirt is **30 pounds now**. You pay 30! 💰

💡 **Remember:** The first price is often the **old** price. Look for **was**, **now**, or **discount**.

Let's try one more:

> **A:** How much is the jacket?
> **B:** It was ninety dollars. Now it is sixty dollars.
> **A:** And the hat?
> **B:** It's fifteen dollars.

**1. Jacket** ❌ Not 90. You made the same mistake again, but that's okay. Let's learn a trick! 😊

> It **was** ninety dollars. **Now** it is sixty dollars.

- **was** → old price → 90 ❌ (not today!)
- **now** → new price → **60** ✅

So the jacket is **60 dollars now**.

🔑 **Trick:** Don't choose the **first** price. Find the word **now**. The price after **now** is the price you pay!

Let's try again. Find **now** first! 👀

> **A:** How much are the shoes?
> **B:** They were eighty pounds. Now they are forty pounds.
> **A:** And the scarf?
> **B:** It's fourteen pounds.

**Questions:**

2. How much is the scarf?

turns.tutor:

Now the shoes. Let's try a new way, step by step. 😊

turns.learner: Hi! Can you help me practise questions about prices? I always get confused with "how much" and "how many".
turns.tutor:
Sure! Today's goal is to ask prices in a clothes shop.

Here's a simple tip. For a **price**, use **How much**.
"How many" is for counting things, like people or books. It's not for prices.

- One thing: **How much is** + noun
- More than one: **How much are** + noun

Here's my own example: You see cool trainers in a shop. You ask: *"How much are these trainers?"*

Now you try. Correct this question:
**"How much cost this hat?"**

turns.learner: How much *costs* this hat? Is it "How much does this hat cost?" Hmm, I think "How much cost this hat" is right because "how much" is for price, so I just need to add "costs"?
turns.tutor:
You're thinking about the right thing: **How much** is for price.

Here's the feedback:

- "How much **costs** this hat?" is **not correct**.
- "How much **cost** this hat?" is **not correct**.
- "How much **does** this hat **cost**?" **is correct.** With the verb *cost*, the question needs **does**.

In today's lesson there is an easier way. Use **is**, and you don't need "cost" at all.

Your next step: write the question again with **How much is**...?

turns.learner: Ok, "How much is this hat?" But I still think "How much cost this hat" is correct. Is it?
turns.tutor:
"How much is this hat?" is correct. It uses **is** for one thing, and it is a full question.

About "How much cost this hat?": no, it is not correct. With a verb like *cost*, an English question needs a helper word. For example: "How much does this pen cost?" So "How much is...?" is the simpler choice in a shop.

Next task:
**You want the same jacket in small. Ask the shop assistant.**

turns.learner: I see, so "How much is this hat?" is correct. But why is "How much cost this hat" wrong? I still think "cost" can go after "how much" directly.
turns.tutor:
Good question. Let's go one tiny step at a time.

In English questions, most verbs need a helper word: **do** or **does**.

Look at my examples:

- Statement: "You **like** pizza."
- Question: "**Do** you **like** pizza?" (not "Like you pizza?")

*Cost* works the same way:

- Statement: "This pen **costs** $2."
- Question: "How much **does** this pen **cost**?"

turns.learner: Hello teacher. Can you help me practise English? I want to understand more difficult sentences, especially when people say things they don't mean. Thank you.

When people "say things they don't mean," that is usually **sarcasm**: the words are positive, but the situation is negative, so the real meaning is the opposite.

Here is an example of my own:

*"Oh, wonderful. The train is late again. I just love waiting for an hour in the cold."*

The words "wonderful" and "love" sound happy. But a late train and the cold are bad things. So the writer is **sarcastic**, and the purpose is to **complain**.

A useful clue: look for positive words next to a bad situation.

Your turn. Read this message from a customer:

*"Thanks so much for delivering my sofa to the wrong address. Really great service."*

Is the tone **sarcastic** or **sincere**? Write one word, and name the words that helped you decide.

The gap is that you looked at **only** the words, not at the **situation** the customer describes. Tone often depends on both.

Look again at this part of the message:

*"...delivering my sofa **to the wrong address**."*

Think about it as the customer: where is your sofa now, and how would you feel about that?

Then read the whole message one more time and decide again: is the tone **sarcastic** or **sincere**? Give one word, plus one short reason.

turns.tutor:
You noticed the important detail: "The sofa is at wrong address." That detail is the key. Let's go one small step at a time.

**The rule:** when the words are nice and the situation is **good**, the tone is usually **sincere**. When the words are nice but the situation is **bad**, the writer usually means the opposite. That is **sarcastic**.

(For the whole lesson: a writer's **purpose** can be to inform, persuade, warn or complain. The **tone** can be sincere, sarcastic or formal.)

Two examples of my own, both with "thanks":

- *"Thanks for fixing my phone. It works perfectly now."* Nice words, good situation. The writer is sincere.
- *"Thanks for fixing my phone. Now it won't turn on at all."* Nice words, bad situation. The writer means the opposite. This is sarcastic.

turns.learner: Hello! Can you help me practise English? I want to practise past simple. I am not very good at it yet.
turns.tutor:
Yes, let's practise the past simple together.

**Our goal today:** use the past simple for actions at a **finished time** in the past. Later, we'll compare it with the present perfect.

We usually use the past simple with time words like:
- *yesterday, last year, in 2010, two weeks ago*

The time is finished, so the action is finished too.

Here is an example from the course:
*I **lived** in Rome in 2010.*

"In 2010" is a finished time, so we use **lived** (past simple).

Regular verbs usually add **-ed** (*work → worked*). Many common verbs are irregular (*go → went*).

Now try this from the lesson:

Complete: "We ___ (move) to this street in 2018." Write the verb.

Then tell me which words in the sentence helped you choose.

turns.learner: I moved to this street in 2018. The words "in 2018" helped me. I think it is finished time.
turns.tutor:
Your reason is also right: "in 2018" is a finished time, so the past simple fits.

One small note: the sentence starts with "We", not "I". The verb stays the same, so your answer works.

Now let's look at the other side of the lesson. Here is the next exercise from the course:

Complete: "She ___ (have) this car since March." Write the verb phrase.

After you answer, tell me which word in the sentence helped you choose, and how it is different from "in 2018".

turns.learner:
I think she had this car since March.

The word "since" helped me. "March" is a time too, like "in 2018", so it is finished.
turns.tutor:
You found the key word: **"since"** is the word that decides this sentence. The verb you chose doesn't fit, so let's look at what "since" means.

"In 2018" names a **finished time**. "Since March" names a **starting point**: from March **until now**. The action began then and is still true today.

**The rule for this lesson:**
- Finished time (*in 2018, yesterday, two years ago*) → **past simple**
- From the past until now, with **for** + a length of time or **since** + a starting point → **present perfect** (*have/has* + past participle)

**My example:**
- *I **worked** in a bank in 2015.* (finished, I don't work there now)
- *I **have worked** in this bank since 2015.* (I started in 2015 and still work there)

Now look again at your sentence. Does she still have the car today? Write the verb phrase again, and tell me why in your own words.

turns.learner: Yes, she still has the car. I think she had this car since March, because March is in the past. The car started before, so I use had.
turns.tutor:
You are right that **she still has the car**. That fact decides the tense.

The problem is the idea "it started in the past, so I use the past simple." Many actions start in the past. What matters is **when they end**.

**The rule:**
- The action is **finished** (it ended in the past) → **past simple**
- The action **started in the past and is still true now** (often with *for* or *since*) → **present perfect** (*have/has* + past participle)

**My example, with a different verb:**
- *I **knew** Tom at school.* (finished: we lost contact)
- *I **have known** Tom since 2019.* (we met in 2019 and are still friends now)

Now try your sentence again in two small steps:
1. Is the subject "she" used with *have* or *has*?
2. What is the past participle of *have*?

Then write the full verb phrase.

turns.learner:
She has had this car since March.

I think "has" because she is one person. The past participle of have is "had". I didn't know the past participle was the same as the past simple. Is that right?
turns.tutor:
Yes, **"She has had this car since March"** is correct. Both of your steps were right:
1. **has**, because "she" is one person
2. **had**, the past participle

**Your question:** Yes, for *have*, the past simple and the past participle are the same word: *have → had → had*.

This is also true for all regular verbs (*move → moved → moved*). But many irregular verbs have two different forms, for example *go → went → gone* and *see → saw → seen*. So it's a good idea to learn all three forms together.

**Recap, using your own words:**
- "in 2018" is a **finished time**, so we use the past simple (*moved*).

Tell me the rule in your own words.

turns.learner: I think past simple is for things that finished. But my neighbour, I knew for ten years. Still I know him now. So I use past simple, yes?
turns.tutor:
The first part of your rule is right: **past simple is for things that finished.**

The problem is the next step. You say, "Still I know him now." So the knowing has **not** finished. That means the past simple does not fit this sentence.

**The rule:**
- The action ended in the past → **past simple**
- The action started in the past and is **still true now** (often with *for* or *since*) → **present perfect** (*have/has* + past participle)

**My example:**
- *She **studied** French for two years.* (she stopped)
- *She **has studied** French for two years.* (she is still studying)

**Recap, using your words:** "in 2018" is a finished time, so we use the past simple. With "since March," she still has the car, so we use the present perfect.

Now rewrite your neighbour sentence. Then tell me the rule in your own words.

teaching.notes:
I am still sure: I knew my neighbour for ten years. Past simple is for things that finished, yes?

Rule for me now: Past simple is for things that finished. If I say "for ten years," I use past simple too.

turns.learner: Hello teacher. Can you help me practise reading? I want to understand texts better. Please help me with guessing answers from a short story.
turns.tutor:
Hello! Yes, let's practise.

**Our goal:** work out what a text *suggests* but does not say directly. We call this **inferring**.

One important point: inferring is not free guessing. A good inference always comes from **clues** in the text, and you can point to those clues as **evidence**.

Here is an example of my own:

> *Maria looked at her watch again and tapped her foot. The bus was still not there.*

The text does not say "Maria was impatient." But the clues (looking at her watch *again*, tapping her foot) **suggest** she was impatient or worried about being late.

Now let's see where you are. Read this short text (also my own example):

> *Tom opened the fridge, sighed, and closed it again. Then he picked up his phone and searched for pizza places nearby.*

**Your task:** What can you infer about the fridge? Write one sentence, and name **one clue** from the text that supports your idea.

turns.learner: Hello teacher. Maybe the fridge is empty. Tom is hungry and he wants pizza. Clue: he opens the fridge. Maybe the fridge is very big too and it is a new fridge from the shop.
turns.tutor:
Your main inference, "Maybe the fridge is empty", is supported by the text. "Tom is hungry" also fits.

Two things to work on:

1. **The clue is weak.** "He opens the fridge" does not suggest it is empty. People open full fridges too. A strong clue is one that points to *your* idea and not to many other ideas.
2. **"The fridge is very big" and "a new fridge from the shop"** have no clues in the text. Nothing tells us its size or age. These are guesses without evidence, so a careful reader leaves them out.

**Next step:** Look again at what Tom does *after* he opens the fridge, and at what he does with his phone.

Which word or action is a **stronger clue** that the fridge is empty? Write it and explain in one sentence why it supports your idea.

turns.learner: Maybe the clue is "he searches for pizza places." Empty fridge, so he wants pizza. But I still think the fridge is maybe new from the shop.
turns.tutor:
**Your clue works.** "He searched for pizza places" is strong evidence. If there were food in the fridge, he probably wouldn't look for a restaurant. That's real inferring: idea plus clue.

(Another clue supports it too: he **sighed**, which suggests disappointment.)

**The part that still needs work:** "the fridge is maybe new from the shop."

Here is a simple test for any inference:

> **Can I point to words in the text that support it?**
> Yes → keep it. No → reject it.

For example, if the text said *"Tom took the plastic off his fridge,"* then "new" would be a supported inference. But our text doesn't say that.

**Your task:** Apply the test to your "new fridge" idea. Which words in the text support it? If you can't find any, write one sentence explaining why a careful reader should reject it.

turns.learner: Maybe there are no words. But I think it is new because the fridge is very clean and white.
turns.tutor:
**"Maybe there are no words"** is correct. The text never says the fridge is new.

The problem is in the next step. **"Very clean and white"** is also not in the text. Those details come from your imagination, not from the story. So they can't be evidence.

**The general rule:**
An inference is supported only by words that are **really in the text**. A detail we picture in our head is not a clue, so we can't use it to support another guess.

**A contrast example (my own):**

> *Lena put on her running shoes and filled her water bottle.*

- "Lena is going to exercise" → **keep**. Clues: *running shoes*, *water bottle*.
- "Her shoes are expensive" → **reject**. The text never describes the shoes. That detail comes only from the reader.

**Your task:** Use this rule on your "new fridge" idea. In your own words, write one or two sentences that say whether a careful reader should keep it or reject it, and why. Also say what is wrong with using "clean and white" as support.

turns.learner: Teacher, I think maybe the fridge is new. It is clean and white, so I keep it. Maybe the text not say, but I see it in my head.
turns.tutor:
Your sentence "Maybe the text not say" shows the key point. If the text does not say it, a careful reader does not keep it.

**"I see it in my head"** is imagination, not evidence. Picturing a story is normal and helpful. But when we **infer**, we only use clues that are in the words on the page. Anyone reading the same text should be able to point to the same evidence.

Quick recap of the rule, using your own work:

- **Keep** an idea when words in the text support it. You did this with "he searches for pizza places", so the fridge is probably empty.
- **Reject** an idea when the support comes only from your head, like "clean and white", so "new fridge" goes.

**Tell me the rule in your own words.**

turns.learner: Teacher, I think maybe the rule is: if the text say it, keep. If not, no keep. My head is not clue.
turns.tutor:
**"My head is not clue"** is correct. This is the reason "new fridge" is rejected.

One part needs a small change: **"if the text say it, keep."**

Remember the fridge. The text never *says* "the fridge is empty." But we kept that idea. Why? Because clues in the text (*sighed*, *searched for pizza places*) **suggest** it.

So the test is not "Does the text say it?" The test is "Do clues in the text **support** it?"

**Your task:** Say your rule again. Change only the first part, and use the word **clue** or **suggest**.

teaching.notes: Teacher, my rule now: if clues in the text suggest it, I keep it. If only my head sees it, no keep.

turns.learner: I want to practise vocabulary in reading, please help me. I think I am good at guessing words from how they look.
turns.tutor:
Good plan. In this lesson, the goal is to **work out the meaning of an unknown word from the words and sentences around it**. This is called using **context clues**.

Looking at the word itself (its shape or parts) can help. But some words look like other words, or have more than one meaning. So the sentence around the word is usually the stronger clue.

Here is a quick task to find your starting point. This is my own example:

*After the long hike, Sara was **famished**, so she ate two big plates of pasta and still wanted more.*

1. What do you think **famished** means?
2. Which words in the sentence helped you decide?

Write both parts. The clue words matter as much as the meaning.

turns.learner:
1. I think famished means famous, because it looks like famous.
2. The word that helped me is hike. Hike is also a famous place, I think.
turns.tutor:
Thanks for writing both parts. The meaning "famous" doesn't fit this sentence. The guess came from the word's shape, not from the words around it.

Also, here **hike** means a long walk in nature, not a place.

**The rule:** Use the **clues** in the sentence to guess the **meaning**. Then **test** your guess by putting it in place of the word. If the sentence still makes sense, your guess is probably right. A word's shape can mislead you.

My own example: *Pat was **content** with her small flat; she didn't want a bigger one.* "Content" looks like the content of a book, but the clue "didn't want a bigger one" shows it means *happy with what she has*.

Now look again at the part after **so** in the Sara sentence. What does **famished** mean, and which words show it?

turns.learner: I think famished is... maybe tired? Sara walked a lot. The word so, and she ate two plates.
turns.tutor:
Good change of strategy. This time you used clues from the sentence: **"so"** and **"she ate two plates"**. Those are exactly the right clues.

"Tired" fits the first part ("Sara walked a lot"), but not the part after **so**. Here is the idea:

**The rule:** **So** introduces a result. The meaning of the unknown word should explain *why* that result happened.

My own example: *Ben was **parched**, so he drank three glasses of water.* Drinking a lot of water is the result, so "parched" means *very thirsty*. "Tired" would not explain the drinking.

Now **test** your guess. Put "tired" in place of "famished": *Sara was tired, so she ate two big plates of pasta and still wanted more.* Does the result make sense?

If not, what feeling makes someone eat that much? Give your new meaning and test it in the sentence.

turns.learner: Maybe famished is hungry? Tired doesn't fit the plates. But famous still looks like famished to me.
turns.tutor:
Yes, **hungry** fits. More exactly, *famished* means **very hungry**. Your reasoning works: you tested "tired", saw it doesn't explain eating two plates, and changed your guess. That is the full method: find clues, then test.

About "famous": two words can look alike and still have very different meanings. When the shape and the sentence disagree, trust the sentence.

Now try one on your own. This is my own example:

*The old bridge was **fragile**, so the town closed it and told drivers to use the new road.*

1. What does **fragile** mean here?
2. Which words are your clues?
3. Put your meaning in place of "fragile". Does the sentence still make sense?

turns.learner:
1. I think fragile means old? It looks like fragment, so maybe broken.
2. Clues: old bridge, closed.
3. Broken bridge, closed... yes, I think it makes sense?
turns.tutor:
Your clues are well chosen: **"old bridge"** and **"closed"**. You also tested your meaning in the sentence. That is the full method.

Your meaning is close. "Old" can't be the answer, because the sentence already says the bridge is old. "Broken" is nearer, but the bridge is still standing. **Fragile** means *weak, could break easily*. That explains why the town closed it.

One point to watch: "fragment" helped this time, but "famous" misled you before. A word's shape is only a hint. The sentence decides.

Recap, using your own steps:
- Find **clues** around the word, like "so" and "she ate two plates."
- **Test** your meaning in the sentence. If it doesn't fit, as with "tired," change it.

Tell me the rule in your own words.

turns.learner: I think the rule is: look at the words around, like so and closed. Then I put my meaning in the sentence. But fragile still looks like fragment to me, so maybe I am still right sometimes?
turns.tutor:
Your rule has both parts: find **clues** around the word, then **test** your meaning in the sentence.

About your question: yes, sometimes the shape helps. "Fragile" and "fragment" share a root about breaking, so your idea there was useful. But "famished" and "famous" look alike and mean very different things. So use the shape only as a first idea, and let the sentence confirm it.

Remember: look for clues in the words around the unknown word, then test your meaning in the sentence. If it doesn't fit, change it.

Now try this one from the course:

What does "miserable" mean here? A) very happy B) very sad C) very fast. Reply with the letter only.

teaching.notes: C

turns.learner: Hi! Can you help me practise? I want to learn when to use "must" and when to use "should". I think "You must go to the park" is correct for giving advice to my friend.
turns.tutor:
Yes, let's practise! "Must" and "should" aren't part of this lesson, but they connect to it well.

The difference:

- **must** = strong, like a rule or a duty. *Example: "You must show your ticket at the door."*
- **should** = advice, your opinion of a good idea. *Example: "You look tired. You should rest this weekend."*

Your sentence "You must go to the park" is correct grammar, but it sounds like an order, not friendly advice. Your friend might feel pushed.

After this, we can try this lesson's phrases, like *"Why don't we..."*, which make it a friendly invitation.

**Your turn:** Rewrite "You must go to the park" as friendly advice. Add a short reason, as in my example.

turns.learner: I don't understand. Why is "must" not good? My friend needs to go to the park, so I think "must" is correct. Maybe you are wrong?
turns.tutor:
Good question, and you're partly right. "You must go to the park" is **correct grammar**. The question is how it **sounds** to your friend.

Think about who decides:

- **must** = there is no choice. A rule, a law, a doctor's order.
  *Example: "The doctor says you must walk every day."*
- **should** = your friend can choose. It's your opinion.
  *Example: "You should go to the park. The weather is nice."*

So if your friend *really* has a duty (the doctor said so), "must" works. But if going to the park is just a good idea, "must" sounds like you're the boss.

**One small step:** For your friend, is going to the park a **rule** or a **good idea**? Tell me which, and then try your sentence again.

turns.learner: Hmm, I think it is a rule, because my friend needs to go to the park. So I still think must is correct. Maybe should is for people who are not sure?
turns.tutor:
You're right about one thing: if it's **really a rule**, "must" is correct. "You must…" is fine for real rules.

But one idea needs fixing: **"should" isn't for people who aren't sure.** You can be 100% sure and still say "should." It means *I strongly think this is good, but you decide.*

An everyday example:

- Your friend has a bad cough. You're **sure** they need a doctor. → "You **should** see a doctor." (Your strong advice. They decide.)
- The doctor gives them medicine. → "You **must** take it twice a day." (A real instruction from the doctor.)

So the test isn't *how sure you are*. It's **who made the rule**.

**Tiny step:** Who says your friend needs to go to the park: a doctor, a boss, the law, or **you**?

turns.learner: I think... a doctor? Maybe he is sick. So must is correct, yes?
turns.tutor:
Yes. If a **doctor** said it, "must" fits. Your reasoning is right: the doctor made the rule, so it's not your choice.

To make that clear, you can name the doctor:
*"The doctor says you must go out and walk every day."*

But on a normal weekend, a park trip is usually **your idea**, not a rule. Then you don't use "must" or even "should". You **suggest** and do it *together*. That's this lesson, "Weekend plans."

The goal: suggest an activity with **How about...?**, **Let's...** or **Why don't we...?** so it sounds friendly, not like an order.

Let's start with one from the course.

**Correct the suggestion: "How about go to the park?"**

Look at the verb after "How about." What needs to change?

turns.learner: Maybe "How about to go to the park?" Is that correct? But I still think "must" is better for my friend.
turns.tutor:
"How about to go…?" isn't correct yet. The problem is the verb form after "How about". It doesn't take "to + verb". Look again at your verb when you're ready.

About "must": if the doctor really made the rule, "must" works, as you said. But when you plan a free weekend *together*, a suggestion sounds friendlier than an order.

**Recap:**
- **How about + -ing** · **Let's + base verb** · **Why don't we + base verb**
- Example: "How about **cooking** dinner?" not "How about **to cook** dinner?"

These phrases leave the choice to your friend, so they suggest instead of ordering.

**Tell me the rule in your own words.**

turns.learner: YOU: Ok, so "How about" + go... no, "How about going to the park?" Yes? And "must" is for doctor, right?
turns.tutor:
Yes, **"How about going to the park?"** is correct. You changed "go" to the **-ing** form, which is what "How about" needs. It's also a friendly suggestion, not an order.

About "must": yes, it fits a **real rule**, for example from a doctor, a boss or the law. For a free weekend plan that's just your idea, a suggestion usually sounds better.

**Recap:**
- **How about + -ing** ("How about going…?"), **Let's + base verb**, **Why don't we + base verb**
- These phrases leave the choice to your friend, so you suggest instead of giving an order.

Now try all three together. **Tell me the rule in your own words.** Include which verb form comes after each phrase.

teaching.notes:
**My note to myself:**
- "Must" is for real rules, like a doctor's order. My friend needs to go to the park, so I still think "You must go" is right.
- "How about" takes -ing: "How about going to the park?" Let's and Why don't we take the base verb.

turns.learner: Hello teacher. Please help me practise English. I want to understand when people say something good but mean something bad. Can you help me?
turns.tutor:
Yes, I can help. This is called **sarcasm**: the words sound positive, but the speaker means the opposite. It is usually a way to show they are **annoyed**.

**Today's goal:** read how a speaker feels from their word choice, not only from the literal meaning.

Here is an example from your course:

> A: Oh brilliant, it is raining again.

"Brilliant" is a positive word, but rain is bad news. The word "again" shows it keeps happening. So A is not pleased. A is sarcastic and annoyed.

**Clues that often signal sarcasm:**
- a strong positive word (*brilliant, great, perfect, lovely*)
- a situation that is clearly bad
- words like *again* or *just what I needed*

**Your turn.** Here is my own example:

> B: Great. My train is cancelled. Just what I needed today.

Is B pleased or sarcastic? Which words helped you decide?

turns.learner: Hmm, I think B is pleased. "Great" is good, so B is happy about the train. Maybe the train is cancelled and B likes that? The word "great" helps me decide.
turns.tutor:

A paragraph usually works like this:
- The **topic sentence** comes first and gives the main idea.
- **Supporting sentences** explain that idea, often with *because*, *for example* or *also*.

Here is my own example:
*Cooking at home saves money. Restaurant meals cost much more because you pay for the service. For example, a pizza at home can cost half the price.*

Look at your sentences, "I read before sleep. Books are cheap." Each is clear, but they share no main idea yet, so they aren't connected as a paragraph.

turns.tutor:
"Sleep is good." works as a topic sentence. It includes the word *sleep* and states a main idea. You could make it stronger later by saying *how* sleep is good, but it does the job.

Your second sentence, "I sleep eight hours.", is a fact about you. It doesn't yet explain *why* sleep is good, so it doesn't support the main idea. A supporting sentence gives a reason or an example.

**The rule:** A supporting sentence shows the main idea is true.
- *for example* gives an example of the benefit
- *because* gives a reason
- *also* adds another point

A sentence that only describes your habit usually doesn't support the idea.

- Weak: *For example, I read on the bus.* (just a habit)
- Strong: *For example, reading the news helps you understand the world.* (shows the benefit)
